Issued at 535 AM EST MON NOV 16 2026

Confidence remains high that Eastern Kentucky will experience 
seasonably quiet sensible weather conditions through at least 
Saturday. The forecast guidance suite collectively resolves the 
region under the influence of a synoptic ridging pattern in this 
time frame, with the respective mid-/upper-atmospheric features 
reaching peak amplitude around midweek. LREF mean 500mb geopotential 
heights climb towards the 99th percentile of model climatology over 
the Ohio River Valley on Wednesday afternoon. Such anomalous values 
affirm the notion that this ridge will dominate the forecast for a 
while, with synoptic scale subsidence reinforcing the dry nature of 
the antecedent airmass. This, in turn, will help suppress 
precipitation chances even as the upper level shortwave pattern 
becomes more active in the latter stages of the period. The ridging 
features are progged to shift east on Thursday and Friday as the 
first shortwave trough simultaneously passes through the Upper 
Midwest. While this shift should yield southwesterly flow and thus 
some marginal moisture return aloft, the continued proximity of a 
surface high pressure system will keep the lower levels of the 
atmosphere dry. So, aside from perhaps a brief increase in mid/upper 
level cloud cover, the effects of this first impulse will be limited 
to the suppression/flattening of the ridge. Mean geopotential 
heights are progged to gradually dwindle down to the 80th percentile 
by Saturday afternoon, and the area will remain on the western 
periphery of a broad surface anticyclone through then. 

Expect daily forecast details to be governed by efficient diurnal 
heating, cooling, and mixing processes for as long as this ridging 
pattern persists. Ample solar insolation should yield above-normal 
highs in the 60s each day, with a few locations approaching the 70 
degree mark once WAA kicks in aloft. Temperatures in the 70s are 
most likely if mixing is deeper than what the baseline NBM guidance 
accounts for, as model soundings depict a stout warm nose over the 
JKL CWA this weekend. Dewpoints should mix out into at least the 30s 
during the afternoon hours, with their exact values playing an 
important mesoscale role in determining the nightly/fog frost 
potential. The area's valleys are poised to decouple after dark, 
with cooler air quickly pooling into lower-elevation locales. Expect 
valley lows near/below freezing each night while ridgetops remain in 
the upper 30s/lower 40s. All of the above should occur under mostly 
fair skies and light/variable surface winds. Such tranquil weather 
conditions are typical for the November dry season here in Eastern 
Kentucky, which also marks secondary fall fire weather season. RH 
values could drop below the critical 25% threshold on the most mixy 
afternoon in the forecast period, so the general public is 
encouraged to pay attention to any local burning restrictions that 
might be issued later this week. If this dry pattern persists for 
longer than this weekend, those restrictions may become more 
commonplace, but long term forecast confidence is not quite high 
enough to lean into that notion quite yet. 

Model spread begins to begins to increase beyond Saturday, when a 
deeper trough is expected to begin ejecting out of the Rockies and 
into the Plains. Members of the forecast guidance suite present 
diverging forecast solutions for both this troughing feature and a 
southern stream shortwave system over the SE CONUS. One camp of 
solutions keeps the leeward trough in a deeper state, which yields a 
period of deeper SW flow and just enough low-level moisture return 
for a few rain showers in the Ohio River Valley on Sunday. Another 
places the forecast area in a regime of rather mundane split flow 
around then, with the Plains system remaining displaced to the north 
in the Great Lakes and the southern stream system passing through 
the Carolinas. Tonight's deterministic NBM favored the former 
solution, with slight-chance PoPs across portions of the CWA to 
close out the period. However, even if those PoPs came to fruition, 
they are not likely to produce a widespread wetting rain. The latest 
LREF data resolves a less than 33% chance for greater than a tenth 
of an inch of rain in the JKL CWA through Sunday night. That data 
gives credence to the idea that it will be difficult for a passing 
shortwave to overcome the antecedent dryness. It will likely take a 
deeper trough with access to Gulf moisture and more robust forcing 
to produce meaningful precipitation in Eastern Kentucky in the wake 
of this dry pattern. Last night's 00z Euro exemplifies such a set-
up, and the next NBM run could feature relatively higher PoPs 
towards the end of the period as a result. However, it takes more
